lesson.title: Double-Shift Detectives
lesson.subtitle: deep → tief, daughter → Tochter — words that needed two rules at once

hook.title: When Two Rules Share One Word
hook.content: Some words could not decide which shift to attend, so they went to both. Deep carried a d AND a p: High German hardened the d to t and breathed the p into f — deep → tief. Daughter carried d and a guttural gh: d → t, gh → ch — daughter → Tochter. Drop became Tropfen, damp became Dampf, and thatch became Dach. These double-shift words look the most foreign and are actually the most rule-abiding: every letter changed according to a law you already know.

footnotes.title: Dead → tot: The Same Rule Twice
footnotes.content: English 'dead' has two d's, and German shifted both: tot. The noun Tod (death) pairs d → t with th → d — death's th arrived by a different route but landed on the same street. One word, two autopsies.

pattern.title: Stack the Rules, Read the Word
pattern.content: Read a double-shift word rule by rule. tief: t (from d) + ie (long vowel) + f (from p) = deep. Tochter: T (d) + och (gh) + ter = daughter. Tropfen: T + ropp... p → pf = drop. Dampf: D → T, p → pf = damp. Dach: th → d, t → ch = thatch (a roof's thatch and a Dach are the same word wearing two spelling systems). Tausend: th → t AND d → t — thousand. The devil is in there too: Teufel shifted its d the same way as devil's cousins.
pattern.linguist_note: Double shifts are your proof that the shift laws are systematic, not coincidences. Wherever two shiftable consonants co-occur, both shift — tief, Tochter, Tropfen, Dampf, Dach, tausend all obey two laws simultaneously.

exercises.prompt: Match the double-shift words with their English twins:
exercises.target_answer: tief, Tochter, Tropfen, Dampf, Dach, Teufel, tausend
exercises.meaning: deep, daughter, drop, damp, roof, devil, thousand
exercises.shift_hint: D → T + P → F / GH → CH
exercises.explanation: Each German word obeyed two shift laws at once — read it rule by rule, devil and thousand included.

exercises.prompt: Which two shifts turn English 'deep' into German 'tief'?
exercises.explanation: Initial d hardened to t, and post-vocalic p breathed into f: d-eep → t-ie-f.

exercises.prompt: Derive the mirror: English 'chew' → German (German kept the k English shifted!):
exercises.english_hint: ch ↔ k — English ran the velar shift here, German never did
exercises.explanation: chew → kauen: English hardened its k into ch (as in speech/beseech), German kept the ancient k. The mirror image of kirk ↔ Kirche — direction is the whole game.

exercises.prompt: What English word is the twin of 'tot' (and of its noun Tod)?
exercises.explanation: dead → tot: both d's hardened to t. Death/Tod run the same story with th → d added.

vocab_hints.note: mein ↔ mine (KJV: 'mine eyes'); -e appears because Tochter is feminine
kalt gains -es before the neuter das Wasser

exercises.explanation: Tochter is a double-shift word, trinken a D→T word, kalt a final-d word — one sentence, three shift histories.

summary.outcome: Decode double-shift words rule by rule and use them in full sentences.
summary.takeaway: When two shiftable consonants share a word, both shift: tief, Tochter, Tropfen, Dampf, Dach, tausend.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the full discrimination gauntlet — all five shifts, both directions, mixed at speed.

twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Meine Tochter trinkt kaltes Wasser" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Double-Shift Detectives without relying on short-term echo.

tief.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and p → f.

tochter.context_phrase: Meine Tochter lernt in der Schule.
tochter.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and gh → ch.

tropfen.context_translation: A drop of water fell down.
tropfen.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and p → pf.

dampf.context_phrase: Aus dem Topf steigt Dampf auf.
dampf.context_translation: Steam rises out of the pot.

dach.context_phrase: Auf dem Dach sitzt ein Vogel.
dach.context_translation: A bird sits on the roof.
dach.etymology_derivation: Double shift: th → d and k/t → ch (thatch ↔ Dach).

tot.etymology_derivation: Double shift: initial d → t and final d → t (dead → tot).

tod.etymology_derivation: d → t and th → d (death ↔ Tod).

tausend.context_translation: The book has a thousand pages.
tausend.etymology_derivation: Initial th → t and final d → t [t].

teufel.context_translation: The devil is in the details.

kauen.context_phrase: Kau dein Essen langsam und gut.
kauen.context_translation: Chew your food slowly and well.
kauen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *keuwan, PIE *ǵyewh₁-; the page lists English chew as cognate — English palatalized the old k to ch, German kept it as k. [wiktionary]

liegen.context_phrase: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
liegen.context_translation: The book lies on the table.

passen.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French passer - the same French verb that gave English pass. [wiktionary][etymonline]

wirklich.etymology_derivation: From wirken 'to act, take effect' + -lich: originally in a working, effective way, hence really. [wiktionary]

wut.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *wodaz, furious — Old English wode, mad: the English d became German t (like day and Tag), and Wednesday keeps the raging name. [wiktionary]

klassenzimmer.etymology_derivation: Klasse + Zimmer — the classroom; Klasse is the same Latin loan as English class, Zimmer originally timber-work, kin to English timber. IPA derived from the verified components (page has none). [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
